ten# Task: M1 — Canvas as a native Mac app

## Context

New project at the repo you are in (project "canvas"). Goal of the project: a local-first
infinite canvas Mac app for the user. Foundation decision is already made and fixed:

- Excalidraw as the canvas engine, embedded via the MIT-licensed npm package
  `@excalidraw/excalidraw` (React component).
- Tauri (v2) as the desktop shell. Rust toolchain is installed on this machine
  (`~/.cargo/env` must be sourced in your shell: `. "$HOME/.cargo/env"`).
- Node v25 and npm 11 are installed.

Why these: tldraw was rejected for its proprietary license with license-key enforcement.
Excalidraw ships text fields, bindable arrows, keyboard shortcuts and dark mode out of
the box — we build only the thin shell around it.

## Milestone M1 (this task)

A Tauri app that:
- opens as a real desktop window (no browser),
- renders a full-window Excalidraw canvas,
- uses dark theme by default,
- runs via the standard dev command (`npm run tauri dev`),
- builds cleanly (`npm run tauri build` may be skipped if signing gets in the way;
  a clean `tauri dev` launch plus a clean frontend `npm run build` is sufficient for M1).

Scope discipline: M1 is ONLY the running canvas window. No file persistence, no sidebar,
no board management — that is M2 and comes later. Keep the surface minimal.

## Requirements

- Scaffold with the official tooling (`npm create tauri-app@latest` or equivalent) using
  React + TypeScript + Vite.
- Embed `@excalidraw/excalidraw` filling the whole window, `theme: dark`.
- No comments and no docstrings anywhere in the code.
- No emojis in code, README, or docs.
- Keep the app shell code minimal — Excalidraw does the work.

## Procedure

1. First reply with your implementation approach in a few lines (stack layout, files you
   will create, anything you see as a risk). Do NOT start implementing yet. Wait for my go.
2. After the go: implement, then test.

## Test

- `npm run build` (frontend) exits 0.
- `cargo check` inside `src-tauri` exits 0.
- Launch `npm run tauri dev`, confirm the window opens and Excalidraw renders  (you can verify via the process running and no errors in the dev output; final visual  verification is done by the user).Commit your work in logical units with single-line typed commit messages (feat/fix/chore),under 72 chars.

Implementation approach:

**Stack layout**
- Scaffold via `npm create tauri-app@latest` choosing React + TypeScript + Vite template, app name `canvas`.
- Project root becomes the Vite/React frontend (`src/`, `index.html`, `package.json`, `vite.config.ts`), with `src-tauri/` holding the Rust shell (Cargo.toml, tauri.conf.json, src/main.rs).

**Files I will create/touch**
- `src/App.tsx` — minimal component rendering `<Excalidraw theme="dark" />` in a full-viewport container, no logic beyond that.
- `src/main.tsx` — standard React root mount (from scaffold, likely untouched).
- `src/App.css` / `index.css` (or inline style) — reset margins, force `html, body, #root` to `100vw/100vh` so Excalidraw fills the window.
- `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` — set window title/size, dev/build commands pointing at Vite.
- `package.json` — add `@excalidraw/excalidraw` dependency.
- `.gitignore` — ensure `node_modules`, `dist`, `src-tauri/target`, plus `debug/` and `logs/` per repo convention are excluded.
- No `DOCS.md` yet unless the resulting module structure warrants it — I'll add a minimal one for `src/` if it holds more than trivial boilerplate; will keep it light given M1 scope.
- No comments/docstrings, no emojis anywhere.

**Risks**
- `@excalidraw/excalidraw` ships its own CSS that must be imported (`@excalidraw/excalidraw/index.css`) or the canvas renders unstyled/broken — need to get that import right.
- Tauri v2 scaffold interactive prompts — will use CLI flags/non-interactive mode to avoid hanging.
- Rust `cargo check` requires sourcing `~/.cargo/env` first in every bash call.
- Node v25 is very new; `@excalidraw/excalidraw` or Vite/Tauri tooling might hit peer-dependency warnings — will use `--legacy-peer-deps` or `--force` only if strictly necessary, and note it.
- Dark theme: Excalidraw's `theme` prop alone may not restyle the outer background (white flash outside canvas) — may need a dark background color on `html/body` to match.
- `tauri dev` is a long-running process; I'll launch it backgrounded with a timeout, capture output, then kill it to verify no errors, rather than leaving it running.

Waiting for your go before implementing.

A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). content.thinking:
I'm thinking about how plain `tsc` handles the "references" field in tsconfig.json — without `--build` mode, it likely just type-checks the included src files directly rather than actually building the referenced projects.

Since tsconfig.json's include only covers "src", vite.config.ts won't be type-checked by tsc, so removing the @ts-expect-error is safe — Vite's esbuild transpilation will handle the runtime import of "node:process" fine without needing @types/node. I can move on now to running npm install and adding excalidraw.

For the src/ documentation, I'm mapping out the flow: index.html loads main.tsx as entry, which mounts App into #root, which in turn renders a full-window dark-themed Excalidraw component. Each module gets brief notes on reads/writes/calls — main.tsx handles DOM mounting via react-dom, App.tsx renders the canvas from @excalidraw/excalidraw, and for App.css I'm considering just noting its purpose (viewport-filling resets) without forcing Reads/Writes/Calls-out sections that don't really apply to styling files, since the guidance favors leaving a section blank over stuffing in a loose fit.

Since this is UI-only and Excalidraw manages its own internal state, I'll note there's no separate shared state module worth documenting.

Moving on to the src-tauri/src/ documentation: this is the Rust/Tauri application shell responsible for creating the desktop window and booting the webview that points at the frontend build, with no real application logic yet for M1. It's a binary crate with no public interface, invoked via cargo run or the bundled executable, and the flow goes from main.rs into lib.rs's run() function, where the Tauri builder starts a window loading either the dev server or the bundled frontend.

Breaking down the modules: main.rs is just five lines that serves as the process entry point, delegating everything to canvas_lib::run(), with no reads or writes of its own, called by the OS launcher and calling into the lib.rs crate. lib.rs is only six lines, building and running the Tauri application with default configuration, reading tauri.conf.json through generate_context!(), writing by opening the native window, called by main.rs, and calling out to the tauri crate itself — with no state owned by this module for M1, since window state is managed entirely by Tauri/wry.

# src-tauri/src/

## Role
Rust side of the Tauri shell. Boots the native window and points its webview at the frontend. Carries no application logic for M1 — no custom commands, no plugins beyond Tauri's defaults.

## Public Interface
Binary crate, no exports for other crates. Entry point is the compiled executable, started via `cargo run` (dev) or the bundled app (build).

## Flow
OS launches the binary -> `main.rs` calls `canvas_lib::run()` -> `lib.rs` builds a default `tauri::Builder`, loads `tauri.conf.json` via `generate_context!()`, and opens the configured window loading the frontend (Vite dev server in dev, bundled `dist/` in a build).

## Modules

### main.rs (5 LOC)

**Purpose:** Process entry point; delegates to the library's `run()`.
**Reads:** nothing.
**Writes:** nothing.
**Called by:** the OS process launcher.
**Calls out:** `canvas_lib` (this crate's `lib.rs`).

### lib.rs (6 LOC)

**Purpose:** Build and run the Tauri application with default configuration.
**Reads:** `../tauri.conf.json` via `tauri::generate_context!()`.
**Writes:** opens the native application window.
**Called by:** `main.rs`.
**Calls out:** `tauri`.

---

## State
No state is owned here for M1. Window lifecycle and webview state are managed entirely by the `tauri`/`wry` runtime.

# M1 — Canvas as a native Mac app ## Scope Scaffold a Tauri v2 + React + TypeScript + Vite app that opens a native desktop window and renders a full-window `@excalidraw/excalidraw` canvas in dark theme. No persistence, no sidebar, no board management — that is M2. ## How the project was scaffolded `npm create tauri-app@latest` refuses to scaffold into a non-empty directory without `-f`, and the repo root already held `README.md`, `.gitignore` and `.git`. Scaffolding directly at the repo root with `-f` risked the tool overwriting or reorganizing those files unpredictably, so the project was instead scaffolded into `/tmp/canvas-scaffold/canvas` and then `rsync`-copied into the repo root, explicitly excluding `.gitignore` and `README.md` so the pre-existing project files were preserved. Command used: ``` npm create tauri-app@latest -- canvas -y -m npm -t react-ts --identifier com.canvas.app --tauri-version 2 ``` Caveat found: `rsync --exclude='.gitignore'` excludes files named `.gitignore` at every depth, not just the root. This silently dropped `src-tauri/.gitignore` (which ignores `/target/` and `/gen/schemas` relative to `src-tauri/`) during the copy. It was not recreated as a separate file; instead its two patterns (`target/` was already covered by the root `.gitignore`, and `gen/schemas` was newly added) were merged into the root `.gitignore`. If a future session re-scaffolds a Tauri subproject the same way, check explicitly for nested `.gitignore` files that `rsync --exclude` may have silently dropped. ## Deviations from the raw scaffold The scaffold ships a demo "greet" flow (Rust `#[tauri::command] fn greet`, a text input + button in `App.tsx`, the `tauri-plugin-opener` plugin, `serde`/`serde_json` deps, React/Vite/Tauri logo assets) that has nothing to do with M1. All of it was removed rather than left dormant, per the task's "keep the surface minimal" instruction: - `src-tauri/src/lib.rs`: dropped the `greet` command and the opener plugin registration, kept only `tauri::Builder::default().run(...)`. - `src-tauri/Cargo.toml`: dropped `tauri-plugin-opener`, `serde`, `serde_json` (unused without the greet command). - `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json`: dropped the `opener:default` permission. - `package.json`: dropped `@tauri-apps/plugin-opener`, added `@excalidraw/excalidraw`. - Deleted `src/assets/react.svg`, `public/vite.svg`, `public/tauri.svg` (now-empty `public/` and `src/assets/` directories removed too). - `App.tsx` reduced to a single `
`. - `index.html`: dropped the favicon `` that pointed at the deleted `vite.svg`. The task also requires "no comments and no docstrings anywhere in the code." The scaffold generates commented boilerplate by default (`main.rs`, `Cargo.toml`, `vite.config.ts`, `App.tsx` all had comments). All of these were stripped. Note this includes `Cargo.toml`, which is arguably "config" rather than "code" — treated it as code per the literal instruction wording ("anywhere in the code"), since the standard doesn't carve out an exception for manifest files. A future session may want to clarify whether `Cargo.toml`/`package.json`/`tsconfig.json` comments count; `tsconfig.json`/`tsconfig.node.json` were left with their scaffold-default JSONC comments untouched because they are not covered by the main `tsc` build (see below) and are pure tool config rather than source — this is an inconsistency worth resolving explicitly if it matters later. ## Peer dependency mismatch: React 19 vs Excalidraw `@excalidraw/excalidraw@0.18.1`'s internal `@radix-ui/*` transitive deps declare `peerDependencies: react ^16.8 || ^17.0 || ^18.0`, and the scaffold pins React 19 (`^19.1.0`). `npm install @excalidraw/excalidraw` completed with a string of `npm warn ERESOLVE overriding peer dependency` warnings (not errors — npm 11's default `--legacy-peer-deps`-like leniency let it through) plus a `sliced@1.0.1: Unsupported` deprecation notice. It installed and both `npm run build` and `npm run tauri dev` worked without runtime errors in this session's testing. This is a real, observed mismatch, not a hypothetical — flagging it so a future session doesn't waste time rediscovering it if some Excalidraw feature (e.g. a Radix-based popover/context menu) misbehaves at runtime. If that happens, the fix is most likely downgrading React to `^18` rather than patching Excalidraw. ## `tsc` does not type-check `vite.config.ts` `package.json`'s `build` script is `tsc && vite build`. The root `tsconfig.json` has `"include": ["src"]`, so `vite.config.ts` (covered instead by `tsconfig.node.json`, which is only wired in via `"references"`) is never type-checked by a plain `tsc` invocation — project references are only built with `tsc -b`. This mattered because the scaffold's `vite.config.ts` had a `// @ts-expect-error type error without @types/node package` comment guarding the `import process from "node:process"` line; removing the comment (per the no-comments rule) did not break `npm run build`, because that line is never type-checked in the first place — it only runs through Vite's untyped esbuild transform. Confirmed by running `npm run build` after the removal: exit 0. ## Verification performed - `npm run build` (frontend): exit 0. Output includes a `chunk-EIO257PC` bundle of ~1.8 MB (~744 KB gzip) and several other chunks over the 500 KB warning threshold — this is Excalidraw's own bundle size (it pulls in Mermaid, KaTeX, i18n locale files, cytoscape, etc. for its "embed diagram" / "embed math" features) and is expected, not a regression to chase in M1. - `cargo check` inside `src-tauri` (after `. "$HOME/.cargo/env"`): exit 0, only the initial cold-compile of ~340 crates, no warnings surfaced in the tail of the output. - `npm run tauri dev`: launched backed by `logs/tauri-dev.log` (this log is gitignored/deleted at session end per convention, not committed). Observed: Vite dev server up on `localhost:1420`, `cargo run` compiled (a separate/first `dev` build from `cargo check`'s, ~15s incremental), then `Running target/debug/canvas`, and the process (`target/debug/canvas`) stayed alive and stable for the duration of the check (no panic/error lines in the log; grep for `error|panic|failed` only matched crate names like `thiserror` compiling, not real errors). Process was killed by PID afterward (`pkill -f` is blocked in this environment as a guard against killing worker sessions — use `pgrep -f ` then `kill ` instead). Actual visual confirmation that Excalidraw renders correctly in the window is left to the user, per the task's own test criteria. ## What M2 will need to touch Board persistence (plain JSON files per the root `README.md`'s stated goal) and a sidebar/board-management UI are explicitly out of scope here and were not started. `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json` will likely need filesystem-related permissions added when M2 introduces file I/O (currently only `core:default`, with `opener:default` removed).

1 # M1 — Canvas as a native Mac app 2 3 ## Scope 4 Scaffold a Tauri v2 + React + TypeScript + Vite app that opens a native desktop window and renders a full-window `@excalidraw/excalidraw` canvas in dark theme. No persistence, no sidebar, no board management — that is M2. 5 6 ## How the project was scaffolded 7 `npm create tauri-app@latest` refuses to scaffold into a non-empty directory without `-f`, and the repo root already held `README.md`, `.gitignore` and `.git`. Scaffolding directly at the repo root with `-f` risked the tool overwriting or reorganizing those files unpredictably, so the project was instead scaffolded into `/tmp/canvas-scaffold/canvas` and then `rsync`-copied into the repo root, explicitly excluding `.gitignore` and `README.md` so the pre-existing project files were preserved. 8 9 Command used: 10 ``` 11 npm create tauri-app@latest -- canvas -y -m npm -t react-ts --identifier com.canvas.app --tauri-version 2 12 ``` 13 14 Caveat found: `rsync --exclude='.gitignore'` excludes files named `.gitignore` at every depth, not just the root. This silently dropped `src-tauri/.gitignore` (which ignores `/target/` and `/gen/schemas` relative to `src-tauri/`) during the copy. It was not recreated as a separate file; instead its two patterns (`target/` was already covered by the root `.gitignore`, and `gen/schemas` was newly added) were merged into the root `.gitignore`. If a future session re-scaffolds a Tauri subproject the same way, check explicitly for nested `.gitignore` files that `rsync --exclude` may have silently dropped. 15 16 ## Deviations from the raw scaffold 17 The scaffold ships a demo "greet" flow (Rust `#[tauri::command] fn greet`, a text input + button in `App.tsx`, the `tauri-plugin-opener` plugin, `serde`/`serde_json` deps, React/Vite/Tauri logo assets) that has nothing to do with M1. All of it was removed rather than left dormant, per the task's "keep the surface minimal" instruction: 18 - `src-tauri/src/lib.rs`: dropped the `greet` command and the opener plugin registration, kept only `tauri::Builder::default().run(...)`. 19 - `src-tauri/Cargo.toml`: dropped `tauri-plugin-opener`, `serde`, `serde_json` (unused without the greet command). 20 - `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json`: dropped the `opener:default` permission. 21 - `package.json`: dropped `@tauri-apps/plugin-opener`, added `@excalidraw/excalidraw`. 22 - Deleted `src/assets/react.svg`, `public/vite.svg`, `public/tauri.svg` (now-empty `public/` and `src/assets/` directories removed too). 23 - `App.tsx` reduced to a single `
`. 24 - `index.html`: dropped the favicon `` that pointed at the deleted `vite.svg`. 25 26 The task also requires "no comments and no docstrings anywhere in the code." The scaffold generates commented boilerplate by default (`main.rs`, `Cargo.toml`, `vite.config.ts`, `App.tsx` all had comments). All of these were stripped. Note this includes `Cargo.toml`, which is arguably "config" rather than "code" — treated it as code per the literal instruction wording ("anywhere in the code"), since the standard doesn't carve out an exception for manifest files. A future session may want to clarify whether `Cargo.toml`/`package.json`/`tsconfig.json` comments count; `tsconfig.json`/`tsconfig.node.json` were left with their scaffold-default JSONC comments untouched because they are not covered by the main `tsc` build (see below) and are pure tool config rather than source — this is an inconsistency worth resolving explicitly if it matters later. 27 28 ## Peer dependency mismatch: React 19 vs Excalidraw 29 `@excalidraw/excalidraw@0.18.1`'s internal `@radix-ui/*` transitive deps declare `peerDependencies: react ^16.8 || ^17.0 || ^18.0`, and the scaffold pins React 19 (`^19.1.0`). `npm install @excalidraw/excalidraw` completed with a string of `npm warn ERESOLVE overriding peer dependency` warnings (not errors — npm 11's default `--legacy-peer-deps`-like leniency let it through) plus a `sliced@1.0.1: Unsupported` deprecation notice. It installed and both `npm run build` and `npm run tauri dev` worked without runtime errors in this session's testing. This is a real, observed mismatch, not a hypothetical — flagging it so a future session doesn't waste time rediscovering it if some Excalidraw feature (e.g. a Radix-based popover/context menu) misbehaves at runtime. If that happens, the fix is most likely downgrading React to `^18` rather than patching Excalidraw. 30 31 ## `tsc` does not type-check `vite.config.ts` 32 `package.json`'s `build` script is `tsc && vite build`. The root `tsconfig.json` has `"include": ["src"]`, so `vite.config.ts` (covered instead by `tsconfig.node.json`, which is only wired in via `"references"`) is never type-checked by a plain `tsc` invocation — project references are only built with `tsc -b`. This mattered because the scaffold's `vite.config.ts` had a `// @ts-expect-error type error without @types/node package` comment guarding the `import process from "node:process"` line; removing the comment (per the no-comments rule) did not break `npm run build`, because that line is never type-checked in the first place — it only runs through Vite's untyped esbuild transform. Confirmed by running `npm run build` after the removal: exit 0. 33 34 ## Verification performed 35 - `npm run build` (frontend): exit 0. Output includes a `chunk-EIO257PC` bundle of ~1.8 MB (~744 KB gzip) and several other chunks over the 500 KB warning threshold — this is Excalidraw's own bundle size (it pulls in Mermaid, KaTeX, i18n locale files, cytoscape, etc. for its "embed diagram" / "embed math" features) and is expected, not a regression to chase in M1. 36 - `cargo check` inside `src-tauri` (after `. "$HOME/.cargo/env"`): exit 0, only the initial cold-compile of ~340 crates, no warnings surfaced in the tail of the output. 37 - `npm run tauri dev`: launched backed by `logs/tauri-dev.log` (this log is gitignored/deleted at session end per convention, not committed). Observed: Vite dev server up on `localhost:1420`, `cargo run` compiled (a separate/first `dev` build from `cargo check`'s, ~15s incremental), then `Running target/debug/canvas`, and the process (`target/debug/canvas`) stayed alive and stable for the duration of the check (no panic/error lines in the log; grep for `error|panic|failed` only matched crate names like `thiserror` compiling, not real errors). Process was killed by PID afterward (`pkill -f` is blocked in this environment as a guard against killing worker sessions — use `pgrep -f ` then `kill ` instead). Actual visual confirmation that Excalidraw renders correctly in the window is left to the user, per the task's own test criteria. 38 39 ## What M2 will need to touch 40 Board persistence (plain JSON files per the root `README.md`'s stated goal) and a sidebar/board-management UI are explicitly out of scope here and were not started. `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json` will likely need filesystem-related permissions added when M2 introduces file I/O (currently only `core:default`, with `opener:default` removed). 41

# src/

## Role
Frontend of the Tauri app. Renders a single full-window Excalidraw canvas as the entire UI. No routing, no other views — this directory is the whole M1 surface.

## Public Interface
`main.tsx` is the entry point loaded by `index.html` via `<script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx">`. Nothing is exported for reuse by other packages.

## Flow
`index.html` loads `main.tsx` -> `main.tsx` mounts `App` into `#root` -> `App` renders a full-viewport `Excalidraw` component in dark theme -> Excalidraw owns all further canvas state and interaction.

## Modules

### main.tsx (9 LOC)

**Purpose:** Mount the React app into the DOM root.
**Reads:** the `#root` DOM element.
**Writes:** the React render tree.
**Called by:** `index.html`.
**Calls out:** `react`, `react-dom`.

### App.tsx (13 LOC)

**Purpose:** Render the full-window, dark-themed Excalidraw canvas.
**Reads:** nothing external.
**Writes:** the rendered DOM tree via React.
**Called by:** `main.tsx`.
**Calls out:** `@excalidraw/excalidraw`.

### App.css (13 LOC)

**Purpose:** Reset `html`/`body`/`#root` sizing so the canvas fills the entire window.
**Reads:** n/a.
**Writes:** n/a.
**Called by:** `App.tsx` (imported).
**Calls out:** none.

---

## State
No application state is owned in this directory for M1. All canvas state (elements, viewport, tool selection) lives inside `@excalidraw/excalidraw`'s own internal state.
---
# src-tauri/src/

## Role
Rust side of the Tauri shell. Boots the native window and points its webview at the frontend. Carries no application logic for M1 — no custom commands, no plugins beyond Tauri's defaults.

## Public Interface
Binary crate, no exports for other crates. Entry point is the compiled executable, started via `cargo run` (dev) or the bundled app (build).

## Flow
OS launches the binary -> `main.rs` calls `canvas_lib::run()` -> `lib.rs` builds a default `tauri::Builder`, loads `tauri.conf.json` via `generate_context!()`, and opens the configured window loading the frontend (Vite dev server in dev, bundled `dist/` in a build).

## Modules

### main.rs (5 LOC)

**Purpose:** Process entry point; delegates to the library's `run()`.
**Reads:** nothing.
**Writes:** nothing.
**Called by:** the OS process launcher.
**Calls out:** `canvas_lib` (this crate's `lib.rs`).

### lib.rs (6 LOC)

**Purpose:** Build and run the Tauri application with default configuration.
**Reads:** `../tauri.conf.json` via `tauri::generate_context!()`.
**Writes:** opens the native application window.
**Called by:** `main.rs`.
**Calls out:** `tauri`.

---

## State
No state is owned here for M1. Window lifecycle and webview state are managed entirely by the `tauri`/`wry` runtime.

# M1 — Canvas as a native Mac app ## Scope Scaffold a Tauri v2 + React + TypeScript + Vite app that opens a native desktop window and renders a full-window `@excalidraw/excalidraw` canvas in dark theme. No persistence, no sidebar, no board management — that is M2. ## How the project was scaffolded `npm create tauri-app@latest` refuses to scaffold into a non-empty directory without `-f`, and the repo root already held `README.md`, `.gitignore` and `.git`. Scaffolding directly at the repo root with `-f` risked the tool overwriting or reorganizing those files unpredictably, so the project was instead scaffolded into `/tmp/canvas-scaffold/canvas` and then `rsync`-copied into the repo root, explicitly excluding `.gitignore` and `README.md` so the pre-existing project files were preserved. Command used: ``` npm create tauri-app@latest -- canvas -y -m npm -t react-ts --identifier com.canvas.app --tauri-version 2 ``` Caveat found: `rsync --exclude='.gitignore'` excludes files named `.gitignore` at every depth, not just the root. This silently dropped `src-tauri/.gitignore` (which ignores `/target/` and `/gen/schemas` relative to `src-tauri/`) during the copy. It was not recreated as a separate file; instead its two patterns (`target/` was already covered by the root `.gitignore`, and `gen/schemas` was newly added) were merged into the root `.gitignore`. If a future session re-scaffolds a Tauri subproject the same way, check explicitly for nested `.gitignore` files that `rsync --exclude` may have silently dropped. ## Deviations from the raw scaffold The scaffold ships a demo "greet" flow (Rust `#[tauri::command] fn greet`, a text input + button in `App.tsx`, the `tauri-plugin-opener` plugin, `serde`/`serde_json` deps, React/Vite/Tauri logo assets) that has nothing to do with M1. All of it was removed rather than left dormant, per the task's "keep the surface minimal" instruction: - `src-tauri/src/lib.rs`: dropped the `greet` command and the opener plugin registration, kept only `tauri::Builder::default().run(...)`. - `src-tauri/Cargo.toml`: dropped `tauri-plugin-opener`, `serde`, `serde_json` (unused without the greet command). - `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json`: dropped the `opener:default` permission. - `package.json`: dropped `@tauri-apps/plugin-opener`, added `@excalidraw/excalidraw`. - Deleted `src/assets/react.svg`, `public/vite.svg`, `public/tauri.svg` (now-empty `public/` and `src/assets/` directories removed too). - `App.tsx` reduced to a single `
`. - `index.html`: dropped the favicon `` that pointed at the deleted `vite.svg`. The task also requires "no comments and no docstrings anywhere in the code." The scaffold generates commented boilerplate by default (`main.rs`, `Cargo.toml`, `vite.config.ts`, `App.tsx`, `tsconfig.json` all had comments). All of these were stripped, including `Cargo.toml` and `tsconfig.json` — treated as code per the literal instruction wording ("anywhere in the code"), since the standard doesn't carve out an exception for manifest/config files. First pass of this session missed `tsconfig.json`'s two JSONC comments (`/* Bundler mode */`, `/* Linting */`), reasoning at the time that it's pure tool config not covered by the main `tsc` build. Review caught this as inconsistent with the `Cargo.toml` treatment; both comments were removed in the immediate follow-up fix. `tsconfig.node.json` never had comments to begin with. Lesson: "no comments anywhere in the code" was underapplied on the first pass to files that don't look like source (manifests, JSONC configs) — check every generated file for comments, not just `.rs`/`.ts`/`.tsx` files, when a scaffold is involved. ## Peer dependency mismatch: React 19 vs Excalidraw `@excalidraw/excalidraw@0.18.1`'s internal `@radix-ui/*` transitive deps declare `peerDependencies: react ^16.8 || ^17.0 || ^18.0`, and the scaffold pins React 19 (`^19.1.0`). `npm install @excalidraw/excalidraw` completed with a string of `npm warn ERESOLVE overriding peer dependency` warnings (not errors — npm 11's default `--legacy-peer-deps`-like leniency let it through) plus a `sliced@1.0.1: Unsupported` deprecation notice. It installed and both `npm run build` and `npm run tauri dev` worked without runtime errors in this session's testing. This is a real, observed mismatch, not a hypothetical — flagging it so a future session doesn't waste time rediscovering it if some Excalidraw feature (e.g. a Radix-based popover/context menu) misbehaves at runtime. If that happens, the fix is most likely downgrading React to `^18` rather than patching Excalidraw. ## `tsc` does not type-check `vite.config.ts` `package.json`'s `build` script is `tsc && vite build`. The root `tsconfig.json` has `"include": ["src"]`, so `vite.config.ts` (covered instead by `tsconfig.node.json`, which is only wired in via `"references"`) is never type-checked by a plain `tsc` invocation — project references are only built with `tsc -b`. This mattered because the scaffold's `vite.config.ts` had a `// @ts-expect-error type error without @types/node package` comment guarding the `import process from "node:process"` line; removing the comment (per the no-comments rule) did not break `npm run build`, because that line is never type-checked in the first place — it only runs through Vite's untyped esbuild transform. message.content: Next task: M2 — Boards as files. Goal: boards persist as plain JSON files in a folder on disk, and the user can manage them from a sidebar. Requirements: 1) Each board is one JSON file (Excalidraw scene data) in a boards folder; propose a sensible default location for a personal Mac app and say why. 2) A minimal sidebar: list boards, create a new board, rename, switch between boards; collapsible so the canvas stays the star. 3) Autosave — changes persist without a save button; debounce as you see fit. 4) The JSON files must stay human- and machine-readable on disk (they will be read by other tools later; no binary, no compression). 5) Tauri capabilities/permissions for file I/O as needed, keep them as narrow as possible. 6) Same code standards as M1: no comments, no emojis, DOCS.md updated, process-docs in canvas_app. As before: reply FIRST with your implementation approach (file layout, state handling, chosen board folder location, risks). Do NOT implement until my go.

content.thinking:
I'm weighing where to store board files before writing any code — since the README describes boards as plain JSON meant to be discoverable by other tools, I'm leaning toward a Documents-based location over the more hidden Application Support folder.

I'll propose `~/Documents/canvas/boards/` given the product name is "canvas", and I need to check the Tauri v2 path and fs plugin APIs to resolve `documentDir()`, join the subpath, and scope filesystem permissions to that folder.

For file format, each board should be one JSON file named by its board ID, storing the standard Excalidraw scene export format so external tools can read it natively rather than wrapping it in a custom envelope. Since the requirement emphasizes readability by other tools, I'll use the filename itself as the board's display name, similar to how typical note apps handle renaming.

Using Excalidraw's own `serializeAsJSON` utility to write files ensures perfect compatibility with the official app and any downstream tool, with `loadFromBlob`/`restore` handling reads. The filename itself doubles as the board's unique ID, so renaming is just a filesystem rename with no separate metadata file needed, and new boards can prompt for a name (defaulting to "Untitled" with auto-increment) before creating an empty scene file.

For autosave, I'd debounce the onChange callback and write to the currently active board's path via a ref to avoid stale closures, while guarding against writes triggered by initial scene loading or board switching to prevent dirty-write loops. Since the format must stay uncompressed and non-binary, I'll write plain JSON text through the fs plugin with pretty-printing.

I'm also thinking about embedded images in Excalidraw scenes -- base64 dataURLs in the files dict are technically binary data encoded as text, but that's inherent to the scene format itself rather than the file's transport encoding, so it should still satisfy the "no binary, no compression" constraint even though it could bloat file size. I'll note this as a minor risk worth flagging.

For the sidebar, I'm planning a minimal collapsible list with create/rename/switch functionality, likely as a separate `Sidebar.tsx` component paired with a `boards.ts` module holding the functional core for listing, creating, renaming, and reading/writing board files. I'm weighing whether the INFRASTRUCTURE/ORCHESTRATOR/FUNCTIONS module conventions from M1 (originally described for Python) should still apply to this TypeScript structure, since the task says to keep the same code standards.

Section comment markers (INFRASTRUCTURE/ORCHESTRATOR/FUNCTIONS) are the only comments allowed, and empty sections get omitted entirely. For M2's more complex logic — board CRUD, autosave, sidebar rendering, load/save orchestration — I need to apply these section markers to TS modules wherever multi-step logic exists, even though React components don't naturally map to this convention.

I'll apply this pattern to pure-logic modules like a boards file for board I/O and a separate autosave/storage module, since those clearly involve multi-step orchestration. For React components like App and Sidebar, I'll keep them minimal and presentational, treating the top-level hook composition in App as its implicit orchestration layer rather than embedding logic directly — consistent with how M1 was already structured.

Now I'm sketching out the module plan: main.tsx stays untouched as the entry point, App.tsx becomes a thin orchestrator wiring a custom useBoards hook to Sidebar and Excalidraw with debounced save forwarding, and boards.ts holds the functional core with pure-ish functions for listing, reading, writing, creating, and renaming boards.

I'm working through what belongs in boards.ts as infrastructure (constants like the boards directory name, default board name, file extension), an orchestrator function like initializeBoards that ensures the directory exists then lists boards, and a set of lower-level helper functions (ensureBoardsDir, listBoardFiles, readBoardFile, writeBoardFile, createBoard, renameBoard, boardPathFor, sanitizeBoardName, uniqueBoardName). I'm also considering whether session-level hook logic should live separately, keeping the orchestrator itself limited to just calling other functions with no embedded logic.

So the decision logic lives in boards.ts/autosave.ts while hooks and components just wire things together. I'm planning Sidebar.tsx as a mostly presentational component receiving props from App, with maybe just local state for editing/collapse toggles, plus corresponding CSS for the sidebar and updated App layout to fit sidebar and canvas side by side. I'm also noting shared constants like default board name, file extension, and debounce delay that need a home.

Following the convention that constants shared across modules belong in a config module, I'll create src/constants.ts as that shared spot. For the Tauri/Rust side, I'm thinking no custom Rust commands are strictly necessary — using the fs plugin directly from JS with scoped capabilities should handle file access without needing custom backend code.

I'm planning the capability scope: limiting file access to just the boards directory using $DOCUMENT/canvas/boards/** as the glob pattern, and adding narrow permissions like allow-mkdir and allow-write-text-file rather than the broad fs:default.

I'm also considering that `documentDir()` from `@tauri-apps/api/path` is a core API rather than a separate plugin, and its permission likely falls under `core:default` or `core:path:default` bundling path resolution for well-known directories. Since I can't verify against live docs, I'll need to proceed with my best recollection of Tauri v2's capability structure.

I'll scope filesystem permissions tightly to just the boards directory, granting read-dir, read-text-file, write-text-file, mkdir, and rename — but skipping delete since removing boards isn't required for this scope. For the default board location, I'm leaning toward `~/Documents/canvas/boards` since Documents is the standard, visible spot for personal creative content on Mac.

iCloud Drive sync is fine to leave as a user choice, so the plain local Documents folder is simplest and needs no extra sandbox entitlements. I'll settle on `~/Documents/canvas/boards`, keeping the lowercase "canvas" naming consistent with the rest of the project, and now I should check whether the Tauri app is sandboxed for the macOS App Store.

Since this isn't necessarily an App Store distribution, I'll assume no sandbox restrictions apply, so plain path access works without additional entitlements — I'll flag this as an assumption. I'll state the default save location directly in my proposal rather than asking the user to choose, and for autosave I'll implement a simple 800ms debounce triggered from Excalidraw's onChange callback, skipping saves when the API isn't ready yet.

I'm keeping the debounce logic itself as a tiny standalone utility — a single generic wrapper function in its own module that takes a save function and delay, and returns a debounced version, since it's simple enough not to need a full orchestrator.

For the boards module, I do want an orchestrator since `loadBoards()` needs to check the directory, list files, and create a default board if none exist, returning a sorted list — that conditional branching between steps fits the orchestrator pattern well. Now I'm sketching out the actual function list boards.ts will need.

I'll set up imports for the file system plugin operations, define constants for the boards directory path and file extension, and figure out the blank scene template structure to use when creating a new board.

I'll keep most constants local to boards.ts since they're only consumed by that orchestrator, exposing behavior through functions rather than raw exported constants, and only promote things to constants.ts if truly needed elsewhere. For the orchestrator itself, I'm sketching loadBoardList() as: ensure the boards directory exists, list board files, and if none exist, create a default board and return it.

Now I'm laying out the supporting functions in call order — resolving the boards directory path, ensuring it exists, listing and filtering board files into descriptors, creating a default board with blank scene JSON, reading/writing board files as JSON, renaming boards via filesystem rename, and sanitizing/uniquifying board names.

Then I'm mapping out how App.tsx wires everything together: on mount it loads the board list, picks an active board, and loads its scene data; the Excalidraw onChange handler debounces saves back to disk; and handlers for creating, renaming, and switching boards each refresh the list and update the active path as needed.

For switching boards specifically, I need to flush any pending debounced save for the old board first to avoid data loss or writing to the wrong file, then read the new board's data. The simplest way to force Excalidraw to reload with new initial data is using `key={activeBoardPath}` on the component to trigger a full remount rather than manually calling imperative update methods — a brief remount is an acceptable tradeoff for much simpler code.

On rename, if the renamed board is currently open, changing the path-based key will trigger an unwanted remount, so I need to flush any pending save first, then update the key/path — since only the filename changes and not the content, the remount will safely re-read the same data with no loss. I also want to think about enforcing unique board names to avoid collisions, similar to how Finder appends "2" to duplicate names.

For collisions on creation I'll auto-append " 2", " 3", etc.; on rename collisions I'll do the same rather than risk silently overwriting another board's file, since destructive overwrites must be avoided. Since board names double as filenames, I also need to sanitize them by stripping invalid characters like `/` and `:` and trimming whitespace — this is a minimal but essential safety measure, not overengineering.

Now I'm turning to the sidebar component's behavior.

The collapse toggle is a small chevron button, with a thin strip shown on the left edge to reopen when collapsed; I'll track this with a simple in-memory `sidebarCollapsed` boolean at the App level, deliberately not persisting it to localStorage since that would be unnecessary scope creep for M2. The board list shows each board's filename (minus extension) as a button, with the active one highlighted, and renaming happens via double-click or an edit icon that turns the label into an inline text input committed on blur or enter. Creating a board is handled by a "+ New Board" button that generates a default, auto-uniquified name.

For layout, I'm switching to a flex row with a fixed-width sidebar (collapsing to 0 width) and a canvas area that fills the remaining space, which means updating App.css so the canvas becomes a flex child instead of assuming full viewport width. I'm also thinking about state ownership, since App.tsx should stay a thin orchestrator that only calls other functions without containing its own logic.

I'm treating React's built-in hooks (useState, useEffect, useCallback) as primitives rather than actual logic, keeping all real decision-making — sanitization, path building, uniqueness checks, JSON structuring — inside pure imported functions from boards.ts. That way App.tsx stays a legitimate orchestrator that just wires hooks together, calls imported functions, and passes data down as props, consistent with a functional core/imperative shell approach.

Given the complexity, I'm considering pulling the hook wiring into a dedicated module like useBoardSession.ts, so App.tsx becomes almost trivial — just invoking the hook and rendering the layout. But I recognize this hook itself would need to house async orchestration logic inside useEffect, which technically isn't pure "state as data" anymore — it's real logic that probably needs extracting further.

To fix this, I'm thinking the effect bodies should be one-liners delegating to imported async functions from boards.ts, keeping the actual work (path handling, sanitization, debounced writes) confined to boards.ts and autosave.ts, while the hook and components remain thin wiring. This feels like a solid, defensible design, though I'm second-guessing the file name — maybe useBoards.ts, bundling both the state hook and re-exported pure functions.

I decide to keep boards.ts as the pure functional core, useBoards.ts as the React hook wiring, Sidebar.tsx presentational, and App.tsx the top-level composition. I also need to remember to update src/DOCS.md afterward with all the new modules, and check whether src-tauri's DOCS.md or lib.rs needs updates too, since a new plugin dependency might be involved.

Now I'm thinking through risks to flag in my reply: the exact Tauri v2 capability JSON syntax for scoping to a dynamic path like the boards directory isn't verified yet and may need empirical iteration; I should confirm whether path resolution needs an explicit `core:path:default` permission beyond what's already granted; and I need to handle the debounce/board-switching race by flushing or canceling pending saves before switching boards or quitting to avoid write conflicts.

Given autosave correctness is a core requirement, losing edits on quit feels like an actual bug rather than an acceptable gap, so I'll keep the debounce interval short (around 400-500ms) to minimize potential data loss, while treating flush-on-quit as a nice-to-have I'll add if cheap rather than a hard blocker for M2.

I'll add a best-effort flush-on-blur/close without over-engineering it. I also need to debounce Excalidraw's onChange since it fires constantly during drags, and guard against saving on the initial mount-triggered change with a "loaded" flag or short delay. Other accepted risks: filename collisions need dedupe logic, large base64 images will bloat JSON but that's fine per requirements, and the React 19/Excalidraw peer-dependency mismatch is already flagged.

I should verify that `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs` exports match what I expect for Tauri v2 (readTextFile, writeTextFile, mkdir, readDir, rename, exists) once it's installed. Given the "keep app shell minimal" ethos and the requirement to keep file I/O permissions as narrow as possible, I'm leaning toward using Tauri's built-in fs plugin directly from JS rather than writing a custom Rust command.

I'll go with the plugin-fs approach since it avoids Rust code entirely and lets capability scoping handle security narrowness, which is exactly what it's for. For debounce I'll propose 500ms after the last change, and I need to handle switching between boards without data loss plus auto-creating a default "Untitled" board on first run. Now I'll write up the proposal covering file layout, state handling, folder choice with reasoning, and risks—without implementing anything yet.

I should also decide on file extension: I'm leaning toward `.excalidraw` over `.json` since it matches Excalidraw's own convention and improves third-party interoperability, while still being clarified as plain UTF-8 JSON text underneath. I'll flag this as a decision point worth confirming rather than just assuming it.

content.text:
## Implementation approach — M2

**Board folder location:** `~/Documents/canvas/boards/`

Reasoning: content the user creates (boards) belongs in `~/Documents`, not `~/Library/Application Support` — Application Support is for internal app state/caches, is hidden from Finder's sidebar by default, and signals "don't touch, app-owned." Since boards are explicitly meant to be readable "by other tools later," they need to sit somewhere the user (and other tools/scripts) can find, browse, back up, or sync (Time Machine, iCloud Drive if the user later moves the folder) without digging into `~/Library`. `~/Documents/canvas/` keeps the app's own subfolder namespaced so it doesn't scatter loose files directly in Documents.

**File format:** one file per board, extension `.excalidraw`, content = the exact scene JSON Excalidraw itself produces (`type`, `version`, `source`, `elements`, `appState`, `files`) via `serializeAsJSON`, pretty-printed (`JSON.stringify(..., null, 2)`). This is plain UTF-8 text and happens to be openable by the official Excalidraw web app and any tool that already understands `.excalidraw` files — no custom envelope. The filename (without extension) is the board's display name; there is no separate metadata/index file. This means: rename = filesystem rename, list = read directory, no ID scheme to keep in sync with a name field. Tradeoff: board names must be sanitized into valid filenames (strip `/` and `:`), and duplicate names get auto-suffixed (`Untitled`, `Untitled 2`, ...) rather than silently overwritten.

**File layout (new/changed):**
- `src/constants.ts` — shared constants: boards subpath, file extension, default board name, debounce delay.
- `src/boards.ts` — Functional Core, no React: path resolution, ensure-dir, list/read/write/create/rename board files, name sanitization/uniqueness. Has an ORCHESTRATOR (`loadBoardList`: ensure dir → list → create default if empty) plus the FUNCTIONS it calls.
- `src/autosave.ts` — one-function debounce factory wrapping a save call; trivial, no orchestrator needed.
- `src/useBoardSession.ts` — the only place with `useState`/`useEffect`; every effect body delegates to a single imported function from `boards.ts`/`autosave.ts` so no branching/business logic lives in the hook itself.
- `src/Sidebar.tsx` + `src/Sidebar.css` — dumb presentational component: board list, active highlight, new/rename controls, collapse toggle. Receives everything as props/callbacks from `App.tsx`.
- `src/App.tsx` — thin composition: calls `useBoardSession()`, renders `Sidebar` + `Excalidraw` (keyed on the active board path so switching boards remounts Excalidraw with fresh `initialData` instead of imperative scene surgery).
- `src/App.css` — flex row layout (sidebar + canvas) replacing the current single full-viewport block.
- `src-tauri/src/lib.rs` — add `.plugin(tauri_plugin_fs::init())`.
- `src-tauri/Cargo.toml` — add `tauri-plugin-fs`.
- `package.json` — add `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs`.
- `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json` — narrow fs permissions (read-dir, read-text-file, write-text-file, mkdir, rename only — no delete, no broad `fs:default`), scoped via path pattern to the boards folder only, not the whole filesystem or even all of Documents.

**Autosave:** debounce Excalidraw's `onChange` at 500ms, guarded so the load-triggered `onChange` right after mounting a board doesn't count as a "change" and trigger a spurious write. On board switch or rename of the currently-open board, flush (or drop, since content is unchanged on rename) the pending debounced write first to avoid writing to the wrong file. I will not attempt a full flush-on-window-close mechanism for M2 — that needs `onCloseRequested` + blocking the close on an async write, which is real added complexity; I'll flag the up-to-500ms unsaved-edits-on-quit window as an accepted, documented limitation unless you want it in scope now.

**Risks:**
- Tauri v2 fs-plugin capability/scope syntax for restricting to a dynamic path (`$DOCUMENT/canvas/boards/**`) — haven't verified exact JSON shape yet, expect some iteration to get `tauri dev` to actually allow it without a permission-denied error.
- `documentDir()` path resolution (from `@tauri-apps/api/path`) may or may not already be covered by the existing `core:default` capability — may need an explicit `core:path:default` permission added.
- Embedded images in a scene are base64 inside the JSON `files` field — still plain text, not binary/compressed, but can make files large. Not a blocker, just flagging since "human-readable" and "large embedded image" are in tension.
- Sanitization/uniqueness on rename could theoretically collide with an existing unrelated file; handled by auto-suffixing rather than overwriting.

Waiting for your go before implementing.

# src/

## Role
Frontend of the Tauri app. Renders the Excalidraw canvas plus a collapsible board sidebar. Boards are plain `.excalidraw` JSON files on disk, autosaved as the user draws. No routing beyond switching the active board.

## Public Interface
`main.tsx` is the entry point loaded by `index.html` via `<script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx">`. Nothing is exported for reuse by other packages.

## Flow
`index.html` loads `main.tsx` -> `main.tsx` mounts `App` -> `App` calls the `useBoardSession` hook, which loads/creates boards on disk (via `boards.ts`) and exposes the active board's scene plus board-management callbacks -> `App` renders `Sidebar` (board list, create, rename, collapse) and `Excalidraw` (canvas, keyed on the active board so switching boards remounts it with fresh data) -> user edits trigger `onChange`, which is debounced (`autosave.ts`) and written back to the active board's file (`boards.ts`).

## Modules

### main.tsx (9 LOC)

**Purpose:** Mount the React app into the DOM root.
**Reads:** the `#root` DOM element.
**Writes:** the React render tree.
**Called by:** `index.html`.
**Calls out:** `react`, `react-dom`.

### App.tsx (35 LOC)

**Purpose:** Compose the sidebar and the canvas around the board session state.
**Reads:** `useBoardSession()` output.
**Writes:** the rendered DOM tree via React.
**Called by:** `main.tsx`.
**Calls out:** `@excalidraw/excalidraw`.

### App.css (20 LOC)

**Purpose:** Lay out the sidebar/canvas as a full-window flex row and reset root sizing.
**Reads:** n/a.
**Writes:** n/a.
**Called by:** `App.tsx` (imported).
**Calls out:** none.

### useBoardSession.ts (144 LOC)

**Purpose:** React hook owning board session state (list, active board, scene data) and wiring load/save/create/rename/switch to `boards.ts` and `autosave.ts`.
**Reads:** board files on disk (indirectly, via `boards.ts`).
**Writes:** board files on disk (indirectly, via `boards.ts`'s save/create/rename); React state.
**Called by:** `App.tsx`.
**Calls out:** `react`, `@excalidraw/excalidraw/types`, `@excalidraw/excalidraw/element/types`.

### boards.ts (103 LOC)

**Purpose:** All board file I/O — list, create, read, save, rename — plus name sanitization/uniqueness, scoped to the boards folder.
**Reads:** `$DOCUMENT/canvas/boards/*.excalidraw`.
**Writes:** `$DOCUMENT/canvas/boards/*.excalidraw`.
**Called by:** `useBoardSession.ts`.
**Calls out:** `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs`, `@excalidraw/excalidraw` (`serializeAsJSON`), `@excalidraw/excalidraw/types`, `@excalidraw/excalidraw/element/types`.

### autosave.ts (41 LOC)

**Purpose:** Generic debounce-with-flush wrapper used to throttle scene saves.
**Reads:** nothing external.
**Writes:** nothing external (calls the injected `save` callback).
**Called by:** `useBoardSession.ts`.
**Calls out:** none.

### constants.ts (4 LOC)

**Purpose:** Shared values for the boards feature: folder name, file extension, default board name, autosave delay.
**Reads:** n/a.
**Writes:** n/a.
**Called by:** `boards.ts`, `useBoardSession.ts`.
**Calls out:** none.

### Sidebar.tsx (87 LOC)

**Purpose:** Collapsible board list UI — select, create, and inline-rename boards.
**Reads:** props passed from `App.tsx`.
**Writes:** the rendered DOM tree via React; local UI state (collapsed, editing).
**Called by:** `App.tsx`.
**Calls out:** none beyond `react`.

### Sidebar.css (78 LOC)

**Purpose:** Dark-themed styling for the sidebar, its collapsed strip, and the inline rename input.
**Reads:** n/a.
**Writes:** n/a.
**Called by:** `Sidebar.tsx` (imported).
**Calls out:** none.

---

## State
`useBoardSession.ts` owns all board session state (board list, active board, loaded scene, ready flag) via `useState`, plus two refs: a "just loaded" guard (skips the spurious `onChange` Excalidraw fires right after mounting a board) and the debounce controller from `autosave.ts`. `Sidebar.tsx` owns its own local, ephemeral UI state (collapsed/expanded, which board is being renamed) — this is not persisted and not shared with `useBoardSession`. `boards.ts` is stateless; every call reads or writes the filesystem directly. Canvas drawing state (elements, viewport, tool selection) still lives entirely inside `@excalidraw/excalidraw`.

## Role
Frontend of the Tauri app. Renders the Excalidraw canvas plus a collapsible board sidebar. Boards are plain `.excalidraw` JSON files on disk, autosaved as the user draws. No routing beyond switching the active board.

## Public Interface
`main.tsx` is the entry point loaded by `index.html` via `<script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx">`. Nothing is exported for reuse by other packages.

## Flow
`index.html` loads `main.tsx` -> `main.tsx` mounts `App` -> `App` calls the `useBoardSession` hook, which loads/creates boards on disk (via `boards.ts`) and exposes the active board's scene plus board-management callbacks -> `App` renders `Sidebar` (board list, create, rename, collapse) and `Excalidraw` (canvas, keyed on the active board so switching boards remounts it with fresh data) -> user edits trigger `onChange`, which is debounced (`autosave.ts`) and written back to the active board's file (`boards.ts`).

## Modules

### main.tsx (9 LOC)

**Purpose:** Mount the React app into the DOM root.
**Reads:** the `#root` DOM element.
**Writes:** the React render tree.
**Called by:** `index.html`.
**Calls out:** `react`, `react-dom`.

### App.tsx (35 LOC)

**Purpose:** Compose the sidebar and the canvas around the board session state.
**Reads:** `useBoardSession()` output.
**Writes:** the rendered DOM tree via React.
**Called by:** `main.tsx`.
**Calls out:** `@excalidraw/excalidraw`.

### App.css (20 LOC)

**Purpose:** Lay out the sidebar/canvas as a full-window flex row and reset root sizing.
**Reads:** n/a.
**Writes:** n/a.
**Called by:** `App.tsx` (imported).
**Calls out:** none.

### useBoardSession.ts (144 LOC)

**Purpose:** React hook owning board session state (list, active board, scene data) and wiring load/save/create/rename/switch to `boards.ts` and `autosave.ts`.
**Reads:** board files on disk (indirectly, via `boards.ts`).
**Writes:** board files on disk (indirectly, via `boards.ts`'s save/create/rename); React state.
**Called by:** `App.tsx`.
**Calls out:** `react`, `@excalidraw/excalidraw/types`, `@excalidraw/excalidraw/element/types`.

### boards.ts (103 LOC)

**Purpose:** All board file I/O — list, create, read, save, rename — plus name sanitization/uniqueness, scoped to the boards folder.
**Reads:** `$DOCUMENT/canvas/boards/*.excalidraw`.
**Writes:** `$DOCUMENT/canvas/boards/*.excalidraw`.
**Called by:** `useBoardSession.ts`.
**Calls out:** `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs`, `@excalidraw/excalidraw` (`serializeAsJSON`), `@excalidraw/excalidraw/types`, `@excalidraw/excalidraw/element/types`.

### autosave.ts (41 LOC)

**Purpose:** Generic debounce-with-flush wrapper used to throttle scene saves.
**Reads:** nothing external.
**Writes:** nothing external (calls the injected `save` callback).
**Called by:** `useBoardSession.ts`.
**Calls out:** none.

### constants.ts (4 LOC)

**Purpose:** Shared values for the boards feature: folder name, file extension, default board name, autosave delay.
**Reads:** n/a.
**Writes:** n/a.
**Called by:** `boards.ts`, `useBoardSession.ts`.
**Calls out:** none.

### Sidebar.tsx (87 LOC)

**Purpose:** Collapsible board list UI — select, create, and inline-rename boards.
**Reads:** props passed from `App.tsx`.
**Writes:** the rendered DOM tree via React; local UI state (collapsed, editing).
**Called by:** `App.tsx`.
**Calls out:** none beyond `react`.

### Sidebar.css (78 LOC)

**Purpose:** Dark-themed styling for the sidebar, its collapsed strip, and the inline rename input.
**Reads:** n/a.
**Writes:** n/a.
**Called by:** `Sidebar.tsx` (imported).
**Calls out:** none.

---

## State
`useBoardSession.ts` owns all board session state (board list, active board, loaded scene, ready flag) via `useState`, plus two refs: a "just loaded" guard (skips the spurious `onChange` Excalidraw fires right after mounting a board) and the debounce controller from `autosave.ts`. `Sidebar.tsx` owns its own local, ephemeral UI state (collapsed/expanded, which board is being renamed) — this is not persisted and not shared with `useBoardSession`. `boards.ts` is stateless; every call reads or writes the filesystem directly. Canvas drawing state (elements, viewport, tool selection) still lives entirely inside `@excalidraw/excalidraw`.

# M2 — Boards as files

## Scope
Boards persist as plain `.excalidraw` JSON files in a folder on disk. A minimal collapsible sidebar lists boards, creates, renames, and switches between them. Changes autosave with a 500ms debounce, no save button. No delete, no board reordering, no multi-window — all explicitly out of scope for M2.

## Board folder location
`~/Documents/canvas/boards/`, resolved via Tauri's `BaseDirectory.Document` (which is `$HOME/Documents` on macOS) plus the relative path `canvas/boards`. Chosen over `~/Library/Application Support` because boards are user content meant to be found, backed up, and read by other tools later — `~/Library` is hidden from Finder by default and semantically means "app-owned, don't touch." `~/Documents/canvas/` namespaces the app's own files inside Documents so they don't scatter loose `.excalidraw` files directly into the user's Documents root.

Verified empirically: before any test run, `~/Documents/canvas` did not exist. First `npm run tauri dev` launch created `~/Documents/canvas/boards/Untitled.excalidraw` automatically, with no permission errors. Confirmed content is pretty-printed, human-readable JSON (see below) with no manual `mkdir` needed by the user.

## File format
One file per board, extension `.excalidraw`, content is exactly what `serializeAsJSON(elements, appState, files, "local")` produces (the same wrapper Excalidraw's own web app writes: `type`, `version`, `source`, `elements`, `appState`, `files`), then round-tripped through `JSON.parse` + `JSON.stringify(..., null, 2)` to guarantee pretty-printing regardless of what `serializeAsJSON` returns internally (I did not inspect its internal formatting — the round-trip makes that irrelevant). Example of an actual blank board written by the app during testing:
```json
{
  "type": "excalidraw",
  "version": 2,
  "source": "http://localhost:1420",
  "elements": [],
  "appState": {
    "gridSize": 20,
    "gridStep": 5,
    "gridModeEnabled": false,
    "viewBackgroundColor": "#ffffff"
  },
  "files": {}
}
```
`source` reflects wherever the running app's origin is (`localhost:1420` in dev; will be the app's asset origin in a production build) — this is Excalidraw's own behavior, not something this codebase controls or should try to normalize.

The filename (without extension) is the board's display name — there is no separate metadata/index file and no board ID scheme. Consequences: rename = filesystem rename (`renameBoard` in `boards.ts`); list = read directory (`listBoardNames`); board names must be sanitized into valid filenames (`/` and `:` replaced with `-`, per `sanitizeBoardName`); and name collisions are resolved by auto-suffixing (`Untitled`, `Untitled 2`, ...) via `uniqueBoardName` rather than silently overwriting — this matters because the underlying `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs` `rename()` call **replaces an existing destination file without error** if you don't dedupe first (confirmed by reading the plugin's own doc comment, not by triggering the bug — flagging as a real, documented risk in the library, not a hypothetical).

## Permission scoping (the narrow part)
Used `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs` (JS) + `tauri-plugin-fs` (Rust), no custom Tauri commands — file I/O goes straight from the frontend through the fs plugin, keeping the Rust shell exactly as thin as M1 left it (`lib.rs` only gained one `.plugin(tauri_plugin_fs::init())` line).

The plugin ships broad pre-built permission sets like `fs:allow-document-read-recursive` that grant access to the **entire** `$DOCUMENT` folder — these were deliberately not used. Instead, `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json` combines the unscoped command permissions (`fs:allow-mkdir`, `fs:allow-read-dir`, `fs:allow-read-text-file`, `fs:allow-write-text-file`, `fs:allow-rename` — each "without pre-configured scope" per the plugin's own permission descriptions) with an explicit `fs:scope` object restricting all of them to exactly `$DOCUMENT/canvas/boards` and `$DOCUMENT/canvas/boards/**`. No `fs:allow-remove` (no delete feature in M2) and no `fs:allow-exists` (unneeded — `mkdir` with `recursive: true` is idempotent, calling `std::fs::create_dir_all` under the hood, so no existence check is needed before creating the boards directory).

Found the exact scope syntax by inspecting the fetched crate source directly (`~/.cargo/registry/src/.../tauri-plugin-fs-2.5.2/permissions/scope.toml` and `permissions/autogenerated/`), not from documentation — there was no internet access in this session. If a future session needs to extend fs permissions, `cargo fetch` the plugin first, then read its own `permissions/` directory — it is the ground truth, more reliable than remembering capability JSON shape from memory.

No `@tauri-apps/api/path` / `core:path` permission was needed at all: `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs` re-exports `BaseDirectory` directly (`export { BaseDirectory } from '@tauri-apps/api/path';` inside the plugin's own `index.js`), so every fs call just takes a relative path (`"canvas/boards"`, `"canvas/boards/Name.excalidraw"`) plus `{ baseDir: BaseDirectory.Document }` — the Rust side resolves the actual absolute path and checks it against the capability's `$DOCUMENT`-relative scope. This sidesteps an open question from the M1 process-docs about whether `core:path` needed to be added explicitly — turned out to be moot, it's never called.

## Autosave and the debounce-cancellation bug I almost shipped
Debounce delay is 500ms, per the go-ahead ("debounce as you see fit"). First draft used a single shared debounced-save instance for the whole session, with the target board name captured fresh on every `onChange` call as an argument (not read from a mutable ref at fire-time) — this part is correct and needs no extra "flush on switch" to avoid writing to the wrong file, because each pending timer already carries the board name it was scheduled for.

The bug I caught before running anything: a *single* debounce instance across the whole app means switching boards, or renaming the currently-open board, can **cancel a still-pending save for the board you're leaving** — `clearTimeout` on the shared timer discards whatever args were pending, silently dropping the last unsaved edit to the board being switched away from (not the 500ms-on-quit case that was explicitly accepted as a limitation; this would be data loss triggered by completely ordinary board-switching). Fixed by giving `createDebouncedSave` a `flush()` method (cancel the timer, immediately run whatever was pending) and calling `flush()` synchronously at the start of every switch-board, create-board (which switches to the new board), and rename-board handler in `useBoardSession.ts`, before doing anything else. Renaming the *active* board specifically needs the flush to happen **before** the `fs.rename()` call, not just before updating React state — otherwise a same-named stale file could get resurrected at the old path if the pending write fires after the rename. Verified this reasoning by re-reading the code, not by reproducing the bug live (never shipped the broken version) — flagging as reasoning-based, not observation-based, since I didn't get to test rapid board-switch-while-drawing by hand (no GUI automation available in this environment, see Testing section).

The "skip the load-triggered `onChange`" guard from the M2 proposal was implemented (`justLoadedRef`, consumed once per board load/switch/create) but I could not confirm from testing whether Excalidraw actually fires a spurious `onChange` right after mounting with `initialData` — the guard is cheap insurance either way and matches what was promised in the approach reply, kept as designed.

## Testing performed (and what could not be tested)
No GUI automation was available in this environment (confirmed in the M1 session too — `osascript`/System Events access failed silently). Everything that follows was verified by direct filesystem inspection around real `npm run tauri dev` runs, not by clicking through the UI:
- `npm run build`: exit 0, no TypeScript errors (checked full log for `error`/`TS\d+`, none found beyond the same pre-existing Excalidraw bundle-size warnings from M1).
- `cargo check` in `src-tauri`: exit 0, clean incremental compile of `tauri-plugin-fs` and its deps.
- First real `tauri dev` launch against a confirmed-nonexistent `~/Documents/canvas`: app created `boards/Untitled.excalidraw` with valid, pretty-printed JSON, no permission-denied errors in the log, process stayed alive and the file's mtime did not change again over ~47s of idle runtime (no autosave loop, no repeated spurious writes).

# M2 — Boards as files

## Scope
Boards persist as plain `.excalidraw` JSON files in a folder on disk. A minimal collapsible sidebar lists boards, creates, renames, and switches between them. Changes autosave with a 500ms debounce, no save button. No delete, no board reordering, no multi-window — all explicitly out of scope for M2.

## Board folder location
`~/Documents/canvas/boards/`, resolved via Tauri's `BaseDirectory.Document` (which is `$HOME/Documents` on macOS) plus the relative path `canvas/boards`. Chosen over `~/Library/Application Support` because boards are user content meant to be found, backed up, and read by other tools later — `~/Library` is hidden from Finder by default and semantically means "app-owned, don't touch." `~/Documents/canvas/` namespaces the app's own files inside Documents so they don't scatter loose `.excalidraw` files directly into the user's Documents root.

Verified empirically: before any test run, `~/Documents/canvas` did not exist. First `npm run tauri dev` launch created `~/Documents/canvas/boards/Untitled.excalidraw` automatically, with no permission errors. Confirmed content is pretty-printed, human-readable JSON (see below) with no manual `mkdir` needed by the user.

## File format
One file per board, extension `.excalidraw`, content is exactly what `serializeAsJSON(elements, appState, files, "local")` produces (the same wrapper Excalidraw's own web app writes: `type`, `version`, `source`, `elements`, `appState`, `files`), then round-tripped through `JSON.parse` + `JSON.stringify(..., null, 2)` to guarantee pretty-printing regardless of what `serializeAsJSON` returns internally (I did not inspect its internal formatting — the round-trip makes that irrelevant). Example of an actual blank board written by the app during testing:
```json
{
  "type": "excalidraw",
  "version": 2,
  "source": "http://localhost:1420",
  "elements": [],
  "appState": {
    "gridSize": 20,
    "gridStep": 5,
    "gridModeEnabled": false,
    "viewBackgroundColor": "#ffffff"
  },
  "files": {}
}
```
`source` reflects wherever the running app's origin is (`localhost:1420` in dev; will be the app's asset origin in a production build) — this is Excalidraw's own behavior, not something this codebase controls or should try to normalize.

The filename (without extension) is the board's display name — there is no separate metadata/index file and no board ID scheme. Consequences: rename = filesystem rename (`renameBoard` in `boards.ts`); list = read directory (`listBoardNames`); board names must be sanitized into valid filenames (`/` and `:` replaced with `-`, per `sanitizeBoardName`); and name collisions are resolved by auto-suffixing (`Untitled`, `Untitled 2`, ...) via `uniqueBoardName` rather than silently overwriting — this matters because the underlying `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs` `rename()` call **replaces an existing destination file without error** if you don't dedupe first (confirmed by reading the plugin's own doc comment, not by triggering the bug — flagging as a real, documented risk in the library, not a hypothetical).

## Permission scoping (the narrow part)
Used `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs` (JS) + `tauri-plugin-fs` (Rust), no custom Tauri commands — file I/O goes straight from the frontend through the fs plugin, keeping the Rust shell exactly as thin as M1 left it (`lib.rs` only gained one `.plugin(tauri_plugin_fs::init())` line).

The plugin ships broad pre-built permission sets like `fs:allow-document-read-recursive` that grant access to the **entire** `$DOCUMENT` folder — these were deliberately not used. Instead, `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json` combines the unscoped command permissions (`fs:allow-mkdir`, `fs:allow-read-dir`, `fs:allow-read-text-file`, `fs:allow-write-text-file`, `fs:allow-rename` — each "without pre-configured scope" per the plugin's own permission descriptions) with an explicit `fs:scope` object restricting all of them to exactly `$DOCUMENT/canvas/boards` and `$DOCUMENT/canvas/boards/**`. No `fs:allow-remove` (no delete feature in M2) and no `fs:allow-exists` (unneeded — `mkdir` with `recursive: true` is idempotent, calling `std::fs::create_dir_all` under the hood, so no existence check is needed before creating the boards directory).

Found the exact scope syntax by inspecting the fetched crate source directly (`~/.cargo/registry/src/.../tauri-plugin-fs-2.5.2/permissions/scope.toml` and `permissions/autogenerated/`), not from documentation — there was no internet access in this session. If a future session needs to extend fs permissions, `cargo fetch` the plugin first, then read its own `permissions/` directory — it is the ground truth, more reliable than remembering capability JSON shape from memory.

No `@tauri-apps/api/path` / `core:path` permission was needed at all: `@tauri-apps/plugin-fs` re-exports `BaseDirectory` directly (`export { BaseDirectory } from '@tauri-apps/api/path';` inside the plugin's own `index.js`), so every fs call just takes a relative path (`"canvas/boards"`, `"canvas/boards/Name.excalidraw"`) plus `{ baseDir: BaseDirectory.Document }` — the Rust side resolves the actual absolute path and checks it against the capability's `$DOCUMENT`-relative scope. This sidesteps an open question from the M1 process-docs about whether `core:path` needed to be added explicitly — turned out to be moot, it's never called.

## Autosave and the debounce-cancellation bug I almost shipped
Debounce delay is 500ms, per the go-ahead ("debounce as you see fit"). First draft used a single shared debounced-save instance for the whole session, with the target board name captured fresh on every `onChange` call as an argument (not read from a mutable ref at fire-time) — this part is correct and needs no extra "flush on switch" to avoid writing to the wrong file, because each pending timer already carries the board name it was scheduled for.

The bug I caught before running anything: a *single* debounce instance across the whole app means switching boards, or renaming the currently-open board, can **cancel a still-pending save for the board you're leaving** — `clearTimeout` on the shared timer discards whatever args were pending, silently dropping the last unsaved edit to the board being switched away from (not the 500ms-on-quit case that was explicitly accepted as a limitation; this would be data loss triggered by completely ordinary board-switching). Renaming the *active* board specifically needs the flush to happen **before** the `fs.rename()` call, not just before updating React state — otherwise a same-named stale file could get resurrected at the old path if the pending write fires after the rename. Verified this reasoning by re-reading the code, not by reproducing the bug live (never shipped the broken version) — flagging as reasoning-based, not observation-based, since I didn't get to test rapid board-switch-while-drawing by hand (no GUI automation available in this environment, see Testing section).

# M2 — Boards as files

## Scope
Boards persist as plain `.excalidraw` JSON files in a folder on disk. A minimal collapsible sidebar lists boards, creates, renames, and switches between them. Changes autosave with a 500ms debounce, no save button. No delete, no board reordering, no multi-window — all explicitly out of scope for M2.

## Code-standards notes specific to this task
`boards.ts` has one `ORCHESTRATOR` (`loadBoardList`) and the rest as `FUNCTIONS` — its other public entry points (`readBoardScene`, `saveBoardScene`, `createBoard`, `renameBoard`) are not reachable from `loadBoardList` itself; they're independent public operations called directly by `useBoardSession.ts`. Treated `boards.ts` as a Functional Core / utility module rather than a single-workflow module, same reasoning as noted for React hooks in general below — the strict "every function reachable from the module's own orchestrator" reading doesn't fit a module with several independent public operations, so reachability was judged at the whole-app level (every function is called from somewhere reachable from `App.tsx`) instead of file-by-file.

`useBoardSession.ts`'s hook function is the closest thing to that module's `ORCHESTRATOR`: it only calls `useState`/`useRef`/`useEffect`/`useCallback` (treated as primitives, like stdlib) and the module's own `FUNCTIONS`, never containing sanitization/path/uniqueness logic itself — all of that lives in `boards.ts`. `Sidebar.tsx` was deliberately **not** given `INFRASTRUCTURE`/`ORCHESTRATOR`/`FUNCTIONS` markers, consistent with how `App.tsx` was treated in M1: a presentational component with a couple of local `useState` toggles isn't a multi-step "workflow" in the sense the section markers are meant for. This is a judgment call carried over from M1, not something verified against a written rule for React specifically — flagging in case a future review disagrees.
